questions.question: What is prop drilling?
options: Passing too many props to one component
Threading a prop through components that do not use it just to reach a deep child
Using props inside an effect
Mutating a prop in a child
questions.explanation: The intermediate components gain a prop they never use, which couples them to data they do not care about.

questions.question: Which approach should you usually try before reaching for context?
options: A global variable
Composition - passing the finished element as a prop
Storing the value on window
Duplicating the state in each child
questions.explanation: Passing an element built where the data already lives removes the drilling without adding a new indirection to trace.

questions.question: When is the default value passed to createContext used?
options: On the first render only
Whenever the provider's value is null
When a consumer has no matching provider above it
Never, it is just documentation
questions.explanation: It is a fallback for a missing provider. That makes a forgotten provider fail silently, which is why a guard in a custom hook is worth writing.

questions.question: Which provider does a component read when several are nested?
options: The outermost one
The nearest one above it in the tree
All of them, merged
The one that rendered most recently
questions.explanation: Context resolves to the closest provider above the consumer, which is what makes overriding a value for a subtree possible.

questions.question: Why does this re-render every consumer on each render of App?
options: Because useState always re-renders children
Because the value is a new object every render, so React sees a changed context value
Because the provider is missing a key
Because setUser changes identity
questions.explanation: React compares the context value by reference. A fresh object literal never matches the previous one, so all consumers re-render. Wrap it in useMemo.

questions.question: Why split state and dispatch into two contexts?
options: It is required by useReducer
dispatch is stable, so components that only dispatch never re-render when the state changes
It makes the reducer run faster
Two contexts allow two providers
questions.explanation: `dispatch` keeps the same identity for the life of the component, so consumers of that context alone are unaffected by state changes.

questions.question: Context is a good fit for which kind of value?
options: A value that changes on every keystroke and is read by hundreds of components
A theme or current user that changes rarely
A value used by exactly one component
Data that only the parent needs
questions.explanation: Context suits values that are widely needed and change rarely. Fast-changing widely-read values cause broad re-renders.
